Open the full Ask Rio Times → Colombia ICC withdrawal talk started in The Hague, not in Bogotá. On 18 August 2026, Caracol Radio said sources at the court expect Colombia to leave the Rome Statute. The government has not confirmed anything, and no legal step has been taken in public. What the Colombia ICC Withdrawal Reports Actually Say The story broke on the morning of 18 August 2026 on Caracol Radio’s 6AM W programme. Its director, Julio Sánchez Cristo, said sources inside the court treat Colombia’s departure as a done deal. Caracol labelled the information extraoficial, meaning unofficial. Infobae Colombia picked it up the same day and stressed that nothing had been confirmed by the state. So the sourcing runs through The Hague rather than through Bogotá. That distinction matters, because the decision would have to be taken in Colombia, not at the court. What Has Not Happened Yet Infobae reported that neither the Presidency nor the Foreign Ministry had published anything confirming a formal procedure. No withdrawal notice was known to have been filed. There is also no bill in the congressional record with a number, an author and a committee. Nothing has been debated, and nothing has been voted. In short, this is reporting about an intention. It is not a law, and it is not yet an official announcement. Who Would Have to Decide Abelardo de la Espriella took office as president on 7 August 2026 after a campaign built on hard-line security. His foreign minister is Ómar Bula Escobar. In July 2026, Bula told Blu Radio that the government would run a very meticulous review of Colombia’s commitments abroad. He named the Rome Statute among them. Yet he also said the plan was not to storm out of the international community. Instead, he framed it as a cost-benefit look at each agreement. How a Country Actually Leaves the Court The ICC is the world’s permanent war crimes court, based in The Hague. It tries genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression when national courts will not or cannot. Article 127 of the Rome Statute sets the exit route. A member sends written notice to the UN Secretary-General, and the withdrawal takes effect one year after he receives it. So there is no instant door. Even a signed decision this month would leave Colombia inside the system until late 2027. Why Leaving Does Not Wipe the Slate Article 127 has a second paragraph that is often skipped. It says a state is not discharged from obligations that arose while it was a member, including money owed. It adds that withdrawal does not affect cooperation with investigations and proceedings that began before the exit date. Matters already before the court also continue. Because of that clause, an exit is a forward-looking act. It does not close files that are already open. How Colombia Joined in the First Place Colombia signed the Rome Statute on 10 December 1998. Congress approved it through Law 742 of 2002, and the Constitutional Court upheld it in ruling C-578 of 30 July 2002. The instrument was deposited on 5 August 2002, and the treaty entered into force for Colombia on 1 November 2002. Membership therefore came with a full domestic legal process. Bogotá also used Article 124, a now-repealed clause that let new members shield war crimes for seven years. That opt-out expired on 1 November 2009. The 2021 Decision That Closed Colombia’s File The ICC prosecutor’s office examined Colombia for 17 years. Prosecutor Karim Khan closed that preliminary examination in Bogotá on 28 October 2021. He signed a cooperation agreement with then-president Iván Duque and said he was satisfied that complementarity was working. That principle leaves cases to national courts when they do the job. Khan singled out progress by domestic bodies, in particular the Special Jurisdiction for Peace. Still, his office kept the right to look again if things changed. The relationship deepened after that. On 7 June 2023, the prosecutor and the government signed an action plan for renewed cooperation. Why the JEP Sits at the Centre The Special Jurisdiction for Peace, known as the JEP, was created by the 2016 peace accord. It judges the worst crimes of the armed conflict and offers reduced, restorative sanctions to those who confess. On 16 September 2025, it issued its first sentence. Seven former members of the FARC secretariat were found responsible for hostage-taking and given eight years of restricted liberty with restorative work. A second landmark ruling hit the army side. Twelve former members of the La Popa Battalion received sanctions of five to eight years over killings passed off as combat deaths. Those killings are the case the JEP counted at 6,402 victims between 2002 and 2008. Because the ICC closed its file on the strength of this court, the JEP’s health is the hinge of the whole argument. Colombian media have reported that De la Espriella wants to dismantle the JEP. Legal scholars quoted in that coverage note the tribunal has constitutional protection. The Washington Pressure Campaign There is a second thread running alongside the reports. On 12 August 2026, US War Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke in Panama City. He announced that Colombia had joined the American-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition as its 19th member. At the coalition forum on 13 August, Hegseth urged members to quit the court. He said he strongly encouraged every A3C member to leave the ICC and reject attempts to rob their governments of sovereignty. Washington’s fight with the court predates Colombia’s new government. It hardened after the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli leaders and probed conduct in Afghanistan. De la Espriella has already turned Colombian foreign policy toward Washington and Israel. His government pulled Colombia’s support from South Africa ‘s genocide case against Israel. That case sits at a different court, the International Court of Justice. The ICC and the ICJ Are Not the Same Court Both sit in The Hague, so the names blur easily. The International Court of Justice settles disputes between states and cannot jail anyone. The International Criminal Court prosecutes individuals. A president, a general or a commander can face charges there, while the state itself is not on trial. For that reason, dropping out of an ICJ case says nothing about ICC membership. They are separate decisions with separate consequences. What Other Countries Have Done The Rome Statute has 125 member states. Despite years of noise about exits, only two have ever completed one. Burundi’s withdrawal took effect on 27 October 2017, and the Philippines followed on 17 March 2019. In both cases, ICC work on earlier conduct carried on. Venezuela deposited its notice on 24 July 2026, so its exit would land on 24 July 2027. Amnesty International noted the existing investigation into crimes against humanity is unaffected. Chad announced its own departure in late July 2026. Hungary, by contrast, notified an exit in June 2025 and then cancelled it. It told the UN on 29 May 2026 that it was staying. What to Watch Next The first hard signal would be a statement from the Casa de Nariño or the Foreign Ministry. The second would be a text sent to the UN Secretary-General. A third test is domestic. Colombia joined the treaty through an act of Congress and a court review. So lawyers will argue about whether leaving needs the same path. Until one of those appears, the honest description is narrow. Reporters in The Hague say a Colombia ICC withdrawal is coming, and the government has said nothing. More: Colombia news in English , every day from The Rio Times. Frequently Asked Questions Has Colombia left the International Criminal Court? No. As of 18 August 2026 there is no confirmed decision, no bill in Congress and no notice to the UN Secretary-General. What exists is a report by Caracol Radio citing sources in The Hague, which the outlet itself called unofficial. How long would a Colombia ICC withdrawal take? Article 127 says withdrawal takes effect one year after the UN Secretary-General receives written notice, unless a later date is set. So Colombia would remain a member for at least a year after any notice. Would leaving stop investigations into Colombians? Not the ones already running. Article 127 keeps a state bound by obligations that arose during membership. Why does the JEP matter here? The ICC prosecutor closed his Colombia preliminary examination in 2021. He did so largely because national justice, and the JEP, was doing the work. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement over migration. Photograph: Wdnet Studio/Alamy View image in fullscreen Questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement over migration. Photograph: Wdnet Studio/Alamy Sweden ‘Absurd, hardline calls’: questions over Sweden’s post-Brexit migration policy Sweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU country Lisa O’Carroll in Stockholm Fri 11 Sep 2026 13.41 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google He arrived with nothing other than the clothes he wore that morning. Hours later he was banged up in a detention centre close to a Stockholm airport to await deportation. Charles, a former business director from Cambridge, who did not want his full name published, moved to Sweden in 2017 to be with his Swedish wife, Lily, and applied to remain after Brexit , before the deadline of December 2021. But the migration agency rejected his application, and he and his wife have been fighting with the Swedish authorities ever since. In a message passed on by Lily, he said he was the only Briton in the detention centre, where he described being hemmed in by three lines of fences separated by a “no man’s land”. “I arrived here with nothing apart from the clothes I had on,” Charles said. “We were told the meeting … with the border police was to discuss my case. They then said they thought I would abscond, which is why they were going to detain me.” Lily, a lawyer, questioned whether Sweden, considered a global leader in human rights and progressive politics , was now like Afghanistan. “They have hunted us for five years,” she said. Charles could be deported in the next week unless his latest legal challenge delivers a reprieve. He joins a list of 2,490 Britons – of an estimated 14,000 in Sweden – deported from the country between 2020 and 2025, as questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA) over migration. In total, Sweden is responsible for 33% of all British nationals deported from the EU between 2021 and 2025, compared with France, which accounted for 6% of all British deportees, Spain at 3% and Germany at 2%. France deported 450, Spain 250 and Germany 160, while Italy deported just 15 Britons in that period. Different countries collate data in different ways, but Eurostat data suggests the Netherlands is another outlier, with 2,270 Britons deported in the same period. Data shows 2,100 removal orders were also issued in Sweden, though it is not clear how many of these resulted in voluntary departures or progressed to deportations. View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas, 78, walks her dog just hours before she is due to be ‘removed’ from Sweden after 22 years. Photograph: Lisa O’Carroll People served with removal orders include Joyce Thomas , a 78-year-old widow who has been in Sweden for 22 years, and George Mason , a 74-year-old with dementia who has been in Sweden for 25 years, both of whose applications missed the deadline to apply to remain in Sweden post-Brexit. John Sellers , a 34-year-old Briton who has lived in Sweden since he was 10, was deported in January. The cases also raise the question of whether the WA delivers the political promise made by the Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier and others promising citizens should not be collateral damage of Brexit. “The level of protection afforded under EU law must not be watered down. Brexit should not alter the nature of people’s daily lives,” Barnier said in 2017. Nine years on, some have asked if Sweden’s approach has been infected by its apparent lurch to the right more broadly, serving deportations on children and even a 95-year-old Iraqi woman who had lived in Sweden for 20 years. “The number of absurd, hardline calls from the migration department just keeps piling up,” the Swedish author and journalist Martin Gelin wrote this week ahead of the general election on Sunday. British citizens who lived in the country before Brexit have unique protection under the WA, but activists have noted that they appear to be subject to the same treatment as other foreign nationals. View image in fullscreen George Mason, 74, seen here with his daughter Michelle, has been served with a removal notice. Photograph: The Mason family “The question is, has national migration policy affected the way in which they apply the withdrawal agreement in edge cases? And has it affected the culture in Migrationsverket [the migration agency] and perhaps in the courts as they apply the withdrawal agreement?” asked James Savage, the editor of the Local, which recently revealed the pressure applied to Sweden by the European Commission. Family members acting on behalf of Mason turned to the general migration route for residency after the migration agency rejected the withdrawal agreement request for him to remain in the country. The judge’s ruling was clear: “The state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Horace [George] Mason’s interest in continuing to reside [in Sweden].” Since the surge in publicity surrounding deportations of British citizens in Sweden, all three opposition parties have pledged new laws to reopen the application process for Britons, and the incumbent government has said it would look at doing the same. Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party, has promised new laws if his party retains power. “Some of these cases are just stupid,” he told the Guardian. “They [the migration agency] should not be lenient, but the present decision-making leans towards deportation.” The Swedish migration agency insists it has only deported 458 British people in strict Brexit-related cases but activists – who have been trying to get granular detail on the remaining cases – say that data may not include Britons who upon rejection from the agency then applied to stay under different routes and ended up with deportation orders. The agency also says there is “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other [EU] member states” and that it has “applied applicable law” with appeal processes. Savage notes that promises to change the law were made three years ago after other cases emerged. David Milstead, who runs the activist group Brits in Sweden, has welcomed promises of action but is concerned that politicians might provide a fix for future British applicants without giving a second chance to those already deported or who have left voluntarily. A spokesperson for the European Commission said: “Correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement is very important to us,” but added: “Reasonable grounds that may justify a late application for beneficiary status are not defined in the withdrawal agreement.” This means “host states have a certain margin of discretion in deciding what they accept as reasonable grounds”. View image in fullscreen ‘Some of these cases are just stupid,’ said Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party. Photograph: Centerpartie, Sweden In other words, Sweden has not breached the withdrawal agreement but rather is exercising allowable discretion. Catherine Barnard, a professor of EU law at Cambridge University, says the withdrawal agreement is “unique”, as no other member state has ever left the EU, and will take time to test. But decisions by migration authorities have to be proven to be “proportionate”. While Swedish courts have not referred their decision-making upwards to the European court of justice, Barnard says a case in the UK may provide precedent for EU citizens affected by the WA. In the case of “CG”, the European court of justice ruled that the UK breached the EU charter of fundamental rights in denying benefits to an EU citizen in Northern Ireland. “In a 2021 case … the court ruled that the charter would apply to those who had moved to another member state before Brexit and lived there,” Barnard said. “While the facts of the case were somewhat different, the principle should remain: the state’s interest in protecting its immigration must be balanced against the rights to family life of vulnerable individuals.” The Swedish migration authorities and police have been approached for comment on the detention of Charles. https://www.dw.com/en/india-s-road-rage-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MxsX The number of cars on India's streets is rising, and over half of all cars sold are SUVs (file photo) Image: Vipin Kumar/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance Advertisement A road altercation in Gurugram, a suburb of New Delhi, went viral last week after a 27-year-old female biker was allegedly chased and hit by a car. The two sides gave differing accounts of the initial dispute, with the car driver telling Indian media that the group of bikers overtook his car and slowed down in front of it. In turn, the motorcycle rider, Shivani Chauhan, said the car was following her and the argument started when she asked the people inside to keep a safe distance. Chauhan's motorcycle-mounted camera shows the car hitting her from the side and them speeding away as she falls and rolls on the road. "I could have suffered serious fractures or internal injuries and even died. Due to such people, the roads of Gurugram and Delhi feel unsafe," Chauhan was quoted as saying by Indian news outlets. According to reports, the driver claims that he lost control of his vehicle and left the scene because he feared reprisals from the biker group. Police have since arrested the driver on charges including attempted murder and stalking. Road rage escalates to violence, shootouts The case was only the latest example of how quickly a dispute on India's increasingly crowded roads can turn violent. In March in Hassan, in the southern Karnataka state, young men reportedly shouted at the driver of a Toyota Fortuner SUV to slow down. Police said the driver turned the vehicle around and rammed the group, killing one man and seriously injuring three others. In the northern city of Dehradun that month, an argument over giving way between two SUVs, a Toyota Fortuner and a Mahindra Scorpio, escalated into a chase and gunfire. The altercation cost the life of one man, a retired Army brigadier Mukesh Joshi, who was not involved in the initial dispute. "The occupants of the Scorpio waited outside the club till early morning and then chased the Fortuner. During the firing, the brigadier, who was out on a morning walk, was hit by a bullet in the chest," said senior superintendent of police Pramendra Dobhal. Concerns over road safety prompted the administration of Daman, a small coastal town north of Mumbai, to take an unusual step. On September 9, officials gathered owners of Mahindra Thar and Toyota Fortuner SUVs and made them take a public road safety pledge. District Collector Saurabh Mishra, the district's top administrator, warned that these kinds of larger vehicles should not be used to intimidate others or display power. More cars, less space on Indian roads India's roads are notoriously dangerous , with government figures showing 485 people were killed in crashes on an average day in 2024. The data also indicates that the number of vehicles is currently growing much faster than the expansion of the road network. Notably, SUVs accounted for about 2.63 million vehicles, or 56% of India's car sales, in the 12 months leading up to March 2026, according to industry data. While more SUVs on the road does not necessarily mean more aggressive driving, the vehicles ' size, height and presence can change the dynamics of a confrontation. "For some drivers it is an expression of strength and domination," former police officer Yashovardhan Azad told DW. "One drives with impunity to make an impression on smaller vehicles," said Azad. He called for tougher policing using new technology, rigorous punishment and a nationwide programme to promote safer driving. "Hitting a smaller vehicle intentionally is not rash driving. It is a measure of criminal intent," he said. 'SUV drivers have a beast in their hands' Road safety expert Prince Singhal, founder of the Community Against Drunken Driving, sees both vehicles and drivers as parts of the problem. "The issue of terror behind SUVs is not just a traffic challenge but also a behavioral issue," Singhal told DW. "The SUV drivers have a beast in their hands and it's their mindset which decides the outcome." How a start-up in India is turning old cars into EVs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Singhal notes that SUVs are a practical choice for bad roads and long journeys, but also points to issues in their design. "High bonnets and elevated bumper heights increased the risk of fatal head and chest injuries for pedestrians, children, and cyclists and all other road users compared to traditional lower cars," added Singhal. With an SUV at hand, drivers often experience "a psychological sense of invincibility," which can lead to hostile behavior, road bullying and rule violations, he said. Are drivers taking traffic too personally? Psychiatrist Ravi Prakash, who studies traffic behavior at Veditha Mind Care Clinic in Bengaluru, agrees that the driver "feels both powerful and protected inside a large, sturdy vehicle." He also warned that there are other mechanisms at play. "There is a psychological phenomenon called 'personalization,' where people interpret an ordinary act by a stranger as something personally directed at them," he told DW. Someone cutting across a lane may be in a hurry. But the other driver may see it as an attempt to assert superiority. A perceived insult can then threaten a person's identity and trigger a spike of anger. "Usually, hitting the other person is not the goal initially," Prakash said. The driver first tries to assert superiority through speeding, honking, gestures or shouting. When that fails, a desire to punish can emerge, what Prakash calls an "illusion of retributive justice." 'Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture' Sociologist Dipankar Gupta says road rage happens "because traffic rules are not strictly enforced," with the problem in no way limited to SUV drivers. "Even motorcyclists get into road rage," he told DW. "It's like a child who is not disciplined and throws a tantrum," Gupta said of the wider breakdown in road discipline. When rules are routinely ignored and people do not want to face the consequences, he added, it becomes similar to "a punch up" in school. Why India will shape the car of the future To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video With cameras everywhere, however, such behavior has become harder to ignore. "The anger is not new. What has changed is that everyone has a camera now, whether it is a dashcam, a helmet camera or a mobile phone," Deepanshu Gupta, cofounder of CrashFree India, a road safety nonprofit, told DW. He warns that recording an incident is not the same as preventing it. "Every driver knows that the odds of facing any real consequence are very low," he said. "Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture. Aggressive driving is normalized here, but culture responds to enforcement," Deepanshu Gupta said. He also noted that road rage is not a specifically defined offense in India, leaving police to choose between rash driving and far more serious charges such as attempted murder. "There is very little in between," he said. In such conditions, responsibility rests on the drivers, particularly when a large vehicle is in a confrontation with a more vulnerable road user. "The bigger the vehicle you bring onto the road, the greater your duty of care has to be," he said.
